title: Verifier‑Assisted versus One‑Shot LLM Intent→Configuration: A Paired NetOpsTraceBench Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed NetOpsTraceBench, a paired comparison of a one‑shot LLM intent→configuration pipeline and a verifier‑assisted generate–validate–repair pipeline on 1,200 intent→config episodes (study_id = rX4f7-1). Using the requested model gpt-5-mini, a deterministic NetOps validator, and Mininet‑style emulation, we applied a preregistered binary episode success rule (validator accepts final config AND emulator shows no availability degradation above tolerance AND no automatic rollback). Of 1,200 planned paired tasks we completed 1,199 pairs. Baseline success = 1,196/1,199 (0.9974979149); guarded success = 1,199/1,199 (1.0). The paired‑success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0025020851 (95% bootstrap percentile CI [0.0000, 0.0058381985], bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10,000); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25. The preregistered power targeted a 5 percentage‑point MDE; given the observed near‑ceiling baseline the study lacked power to detect much smaller absolute gains. Repair was invoked only three times. We explicitly disclose that the preregistered per‑topology confirmatory breakdown (H3) was not executed; archived analysis artifacts contain only aggregated confirmatory results (see analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/results.json). Under the controlled emulation and task‑corpus conditions tested, we observe no statistically significant advantage for the verifier‑assisted pipeline and provide full archived artifacts to support reproducible interpretation.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent expressed in natural language into executable device configurations for network operations (NetOps). Recent surveys and system literature emphasize that operational reliability depends on orchestration, deterministic validators, provenance, and sandboxed execution rather than on the base LLM alone [1,2]. A canonical mitigation strategy is the generate–validate–repair (verifier‑assisted) architecture: an LLM proposes a candidate, an automated verifier checks constraints and safety, and an automated repair loop iterates until the verifier accepts a candidate [3–6]. Despite conceptual support, preregistered, paired evidence measuring whether verifier assistance yields an operationally meaningful improvement (rollback‑aware binary success) relative to one‑shot generation is limited.

We address this gap with NetOpsTraceBench (study_id = rX4f7-1), a preregistered, paired, emulator‑grounded study comparing (A) one‑shot NL→config generation (baseline) and (B) a guarded generate–validate–repair pipeline that shares the same initial candidate per pair. The primary research question (from the preregistration) is: Can a reproducible, workflow‑centered benchmark of paired intent→config episodes produce an objective paired binary success metric that reliably distinguishes verifier‑assisted pipelines from one‑shot generation across two simulated topologies? Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered experimental design and full execution artifacts (rX4f7-1); (2) a paired analysis on 1,199 completed pairs using the requested model gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator; and (3) transparent reporting of an analytic deviation (paired binary inference using exact McNemar + bootstrap CI) and explicit disclosure that the preregistered per‑topology confirmatory breakdown (H3) was not executed and therefore remains untested in the confirmatory analysis.
sections.related_work: Prior surveys and systems work position LLMs as components inside broader AIOps/NetOps workflows and repeatedly highlight that correctness and trustworthiness are properties of the whole orchestration stack (model + verifier + provenance + sandboxed execution), not of the base LLM alone [1,2]. Generate–validate‑repair patterns appear in NL→formal‑spec translation, topology compilation, and domain‑specific misconfiguration detectors; these demonstrations typically show feasibility but evaluate on constructed or domain‑calibrated corpora and depend on verifier strictness [3–10]. Empirical studies document LLM failure modes relevant to NetOps—hallucination, unit/semantic errors, miscalibration, provenance loss, and prompt‑injection susceptibility—motivating external validators and provenance linkers [11–14]. Several prototype NetOps tools report per‑task gains from verifier loops but also note that gains depend on task selection and validator configuration [6–9]. The literature therefore motivates workflow‑centered benchmarks that record full provider and validator traces, include emulator execution to check operational side effects, and preregister analysis choices to reduce researcher degrees of freedom—recommendations that informed our design.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand: We preregistered NetOpsTraceBench (rX4f7-1; preregistration SHA‑256 = 77abe8b493bde44484e0b3d02cfd7f9ec1621ff7e7847889082ae177a7ed5712) and froze confirmatory hypotheses, inclusion/exclusion rules, seeds, stopping rules, and the analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1). The primary estimand is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistration specified paired confirmatory hypotheses H1–H3 (H3: per‑topology concordance check across two simulated topology clusters edge/core).

Task corpus and topology clusters: The benchmark scope defined 1,200 deterministic tasks split into two simulated topology clusters (edge = 600, core = 600). Tasks were produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 (generator_version = 5.0) and include structured fields (initial_state, expected_final_state, required_sequence, workflow_policies, difficulty label). Tasks carry deterministic provenance metadata and are labeled synthetic or consented for contamination control.

Paired generation semantics and pipeline orchestration: To isolate verifier and repair effects while minimizing generation variability we used the preregistered shared_initial_candidate design (generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate"). For each task a single shared initial candidate was produced and used in both the baseline (one‑shot) and guarded (verifier‑assisted) episodes. This design choice intentionally controls for LLM generation variability and focuses the comparison on the verifier/repair intervention (a choice recorded in the preregistration and in execution/model_configuration.json).

Baseline vs guarded: Baseline episodes recorded the single candidate and proceeded to deterministic parsing and emulator checks without invoking automated repair. Guarded episodes fed the same shared initial candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0). If the validator accepted the candidate the episode proceeded to emulation; if rejected the guarded pipeline could invoke a single preregistered automated repair call (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). All repair prompts, provider traces, and repair results were archived.

Deterministic validator, emulator checks, and binary success rule: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces syntactic parsing, required_command_count, workflow_policies, and returns validation_after.valid and structured diagnostics (observed_touched_field_count, violation_codes, difficulty metadata, repair_applied). The preregistered binary episode success requires: (1) validator acceptance of the final configuration (validation_after.valid == true), (2) emulator execution with no availability degradation above preregistered tolerance, and (3) no automatic rollback during simulated execution. Exclusion rules (contamination thresholds, unparsable outputs, emulator failure) are deterministic and logged.

Analysis plan and executed confirmatory test: The preregistration prescribed a paired nonparametric test and bootstrap CI. Because outcomes are binary and archived data concentrated in concordant cells, the executed confirmatory analysis used an exact McNemar two‑sided test on discordant pairs and computed a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI with frozen bootstrap_seed = 1729 and 10,000 resamples. All analysis code, seeds, and inputs are archived. Key archived artifacts for readers are analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/results.json, analysis/analysis_log.jsonl, and execution/execution_manifest.json (these files contain the contingency table, per‑condition counts, estimate, p‑value, CI parameters, provider audit counts, and the analysis log). Researchers can consult those artifacts for exact reproduction.

Status of preregistered topology breakdown (H3): The preregistration included a confirmatory per‑topology breakdown (H3). The archived confirmatory analysis artifacts contain only aggregated paired results; no per‑cluster contingency tables or per‑cluster inferential outputs are present in the archive. Therefore H3 was not executed as a confirmatory subgroup analysis in the archived run. This omission is documented in the analysis artifacts and logs (see analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/analysis_log.jsonl) and is reported here as an explicit, preregistration‑supported disclosure rather than a post‑hoc omission. H3 remains eligible for exploratory follow‑up using the archived raw episode artifacts but was not part of the confirmatory inference reported below.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting: The run completed 2,398 of 2,400 planned episodes and produced 1,199 complete paired observations (complete_pairs = 1,199; failed_episode_count = 2). Provider audit shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 1,203; completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 1,202; failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 1; stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 1,200 and repair = 3 (execution/execution_manifest.json, deterministic_reconciliation.json).

Primary outcome counts and rates: The aggregated paired 2×2 contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is: n11 = 1,196 (both succeeded), n10 = 3 (guarded succeeded while baseline failed), n01 = 0 (baseline succeeded while guarded failed), n00 = 0 (both failed). Baseline_success_count = 1,196 (baseline_success_rate = 1,196/1,199 = 0.9974979149291076); guarded_success_count = 1,199 (guarded_success_rate = 1,199/1,199 = 1.0). Observed paired‑success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002502085070892446.

Confirmatory inference and CI: Exact McNemar two‑sided test on discordant counts (n10 = 3, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.25 (archived in analysis/results.json). Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000) for the paired‑success‑rate difference is [0.0000, 0.005838198498748957] (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl and analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg). The CI lower bound at 0.0 and the small discordant count reflect the concentration of outcomes in concordant successful pairs.

Repair invocation and diagnostics: The guarded pipeline invoked repair only three times (stage_counts.repair = 3). Representative per‑episode scoring artifacts (execution/scoring/*.json) show that the majority of shared_initial_candidates satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 checks (validation_after.valid = true; repair_applied = false). Representative task entries illustrate heterogeneous declared difficulty but frequent initial acceptance of the shared candidate (examples: task-000001 medium; task-000002 hard; task-000003 hard).

Missingness and exclusions: analysis/missingness_summary.csv reports complete_pairs = 1,199; failed_baseline_episodes = 1; failed_guarded_episodes = 1; both_missing_pairs = 1. Contamination checks did not trigger exclusions (analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty). The single pair reduction from 1,200 to 1,199 is recorded in the run manifest and logs.

Interpretation of discordant pattern: All discordant pairs favored guarded (n10 = 3, n01 = 0), but the small absolute discordant count (3/1,199 ≈ 0.25%) yields no statistical significance at the preregistered alpha and produces a bootstrap CI that includes zero. These factual outcomes and diagnostics are reproducible from the archived artifacts cited above.
sections.discussion:
Statistical and operational interpretation: The confirmatory evidence shows no statistically significant advantage for the guarded pipeline under the tested corpus and validator configuration (exact McNemar p = 0.25; 95% bootstrap CI includes zero). Two artifact‑supported explanations are salient. First, near‑ceiling baseline performance (≈99.75%) left little headroom for absolute improvement relative to the preregistered MDE (5 percentage points); the archived contingency counts and CI quantify that limitation. Second, the shared_initial_candidate design combined with the deterministic task generator and a validator configuration that enforces explicit required sequences resulted in a low repair invocation rate (repair = 3), reducing opportunities for the guarded pipeline to show incremental gains on the preregistered binary success metric.

Threats to validity and externality: Internal validity is strengthened by deterministic seeds, frozen task generation, and automated exclusion rules. Construct validity hinges on whether our binary success rule (validator acceptance + emulator availability tolerance + no rollback) captures operational correctness in a production setting. External validity is limited: only the requested model family gpt-5-mini was exercised; tasks were synthetic/consented and vendor‑agnostic; emulation approximates production but may not capture vendor idiosyncrasies, routing convergence dynamics, or transient telemetry. Verifier strictness materially affects outcomes; different validator thresholds could materially change repair rates and measured gains. Finally, the preregistered per‑topology confirmatory hypothesis (H3) was not executed in the archived confirmatory analysis; the archive contains only aggregated confirmatory outputs (see Methodology). This omission is disclosed here and recorded in the analysis log.

Operational implications and recommendations: When initial generation already satisfies deterministic verifier checks on well‑specified tasks, generate–validate–repair will be infrequently exercised and measured gains on a binary success metric will be small. To evaluate verifier value more conclusively, future benchmarks should (a) increase task ambiguity or adversarial content, (b) vary verifier strictness to trade sensitivity vs false rejection, (c) exercise multiple LLM families and vendor renderers, and (d) preregister and report per‑topology (and other subgroup) confirmatory analyses. The archived artifacts provide a reproducible baseline for such sensitivity studies.
sections.conclusion: NetOpsTraceBench provides a preregistered, artifact‑rich paired comparison of one‑shot and verifier‑assisted NL→config pipelines on 1,199 completed pairs using the requested model gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator. Aggregated confirmatory results show a small absolute guarded advantage (≈0.25 percentage points) but no statistical significance (exact McNemar p = 0.25; 95% bootstrap CI includes zero). Repair was rarely invoked (3 calls). We explicitly disclose that the preregistered per‑topology confirmatory breakdown (H3) was not executed in the archived confirmatory analysis; archived artifacts contain only aggregated confirmatory outputs (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/results.json). The null result is best read as evidence that, under the synthetic tasks and validator configuration used here, baseline generation already met deterministic verifier criteria; follow‑ups should target more adversarial and diverse corpora, varied verifier strictness, and multiple LLM families. All run artifacts, seeds, provider traces, validator traces, and analysis code are archived to enable exact reproduction and planned exploratory follow‑up analyses (see Disclosure Statement).

limitations: Single model family tested (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across other LLMs or fine‑tuned variants.
Task corpus skew: synthetic/consented tasks yielded near‑ceiling baseline success (≈99.75%), limiting headroom and statistical power to detect practical improvements by guarded pipelines.

Emulator fidelity: Mininet‑style emulation and deterministic validators approximate production behavior but may not capture all deployment failure modes (routing convergence, vendor idiosyncrasies, transient telemetry).

Verifier configuration dependence: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 acceptance thresholds and parsing rules materially affect outcomes; different verifier strictness could change repair invocation rates and measured gains.

Analytic deviation documented: the preregistration specified a Wilcoxon signed‑rank paired procedure; the archived confirmatory analysis used an exact McNemar test because outcomes were binary. This deviation is recorded in archived analysis artifacts and in the Disclosure Statement above.
Preregistered topology breakdown (H3) status: H3 was preregistered but was not executed in the archived confirmatory analysis; no per‑cluster confirmatory artifacts are present in the archive.
